I got this from Humble for free, but I finished the game and think I should review it.

[b]WARNING: SPOILERS ARE PRESENT IN THIS REVIEW[/b]

[h1]SUMMARY OF THE STORY[/h1]

You are a interrorgator for the company, Orwell. You have to find out who caused 2-3 bombings depending on the way you played the game. In my playthrough, 2 bombs went off and I helped discover and disarm the 3rd.

[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]

You go through different sites finding information on people and try to find out if they cause the bombing or not. You can also access emails, messages, and calls if you find emails, phone numbers, and usernames. You can even find ways of accessing devices such as computers and phones to find evicence and info. 

[h1]OVERALL REVIEW[/h1]

4/5

Story: 5/5
Gameplay Mechanics: 3/5

Although I think the story is REALLY good for this game, the Gameplay Mechanics are meh. Although the UI isn't confusing like Call of Duty: Black Ops 4's HUD in-game, the way it works is too easy for my taste. They highlight the text for you and tell you who it matches up to. It's a great concept, but it wasn't executed correctly in my opinion. Maybe make the user choose which profile it goes to instead of showing them what profile to add it to instead of trying to guide them into the right direction. Example: There's 2 datachunks that conflict with eachother when trying to find the 3rd bomb. The game babies you by showing you which profile it matches to instead of letting you choose. It's kinda like aim assist in COD: it babies you by helping you kill enemies instead of letting you use skill to kill them. Let the person find out theirself instead of telling them, "Oh by the way, this person was planning this. Put it on their profile."

Besides that, the story is really good. All yellow text effects the story of the game, and I really like it when you have to choose. There are multiple endings, which adds to the replayability. Plus, the concept is really good. You try to find out who planted the bomb at the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd location while learning about other information that people have. Through my playthrough, you learn about other lives. You learn about relationships people have, who people have met, who they are friends with, who are they not friends with, etc. It adds to the story in my opinion because some information you get can show why some people have this problem.

[h1]SUMMARY OF WHOLE REVIEW[/h1]

I think it's a really good game with a good story, but game mechanics that I dislike.
Honestly, I loved it. If it sounds boring to you, it probably will be. If it sounds interesting to you, it probably will be.

Wow, what an immersive experience. Orwell is less of a game and more of an intricate story told in a unique way with VN-like decisions that impact how the game plays out. If you don't like reading or slow gameplay, chances are that Orwell is definitely not the game for you.

But if you skip Orwell, you will be missing out on an incredible story with plenty of character development that actually makes them feel like real people. You play as an investigator who invades the private lives of his/her fellow civilians in order to put an end to the recent terrorist bombings. How far will you go in breaking down the boundaries of privacy in order to potentially save lives? Is the privacy of the few more valuable than the lives of even fewer? In Orwell, no choice is as simple as it initially seems, and it's these philosophical and ethical questions that make the game a blast to play through.

There are plenty of great twists in the story and the soundtrack is ambient, though satisfying. Orwell's primary flaw is actually its greatest strength: the plot has such resonance that it makes the game impossible to replay. Don't let that deter you; Orwell is worth every penny.

A really interesting thriller game. Lasts around six hours in a single playthrough (there are three different endings).

Depending on what the player does or doesn't do (and how fast or slowly), different things can happen. For example, whether a certain character gets arrested or killed during the attempt to arrest them depends on what the player decided to (not) do (and how fast) while that attempt is happening.

Apparently, the save file can be transferred to the sequel. The sequel takes place in parallel to this game and if you decide to transfer the save file to it, you're going to see newspaper titles that mirror what happened in your playthrough of this game.

Warning to epileptic people: at two points in the story, the screen starts flashing. It's not very fast/rapid, but it does happen. The second time it happens, it lasts for ten minutes. Definitely something you need to know.

Overall, a really nice game, if you can stomach the fact that it's mostly text and clicking on keywords, static pictures and buttons, as if you were using a computer application.

I nabbed this game for free, expecting some short text-based adventure game. I was sorely mistaken. I was rapidly immersed in the game and its detailed storyline. The interface and art style are clean, intuitive and dare I say beautiful - your interactions with the game are also very quick to learn but not boring to repeat.

Back to the story, however - as the game is tagged, your choices really do matter in influencing what happens throughout the story. However, the same basic endings happen - you get to choose between these regardless of your path, so your choices along the way won't shaft you and prevent an ending. I had multiple eureka moments throughout the game - it kept me on my toes the entire time.

The game is structured in a 'chapter' format, with each chapter being a day in the game. If you're not a fan of this sort of format, the game might not be for you.

Overall, however, I'd thoroughly recomend the game - picking this one up for free has encouraged me to buy the second episode, which I guess is proof of how much I enjoyed it.

Intresting premise,  poor execution. In the attempt to create stakes for the players decision, Orwell goes out of it's way to obfuscate or even fail to present clarfying information until after the decision is made. It also prevents refinement of past data with new context. Being forced to compete in the 20 meter jump to conclusions in order to find the context you needed to make that conclusion is beyond obxnoxious. This is made worse by there being minimal clarity to what the data you've supplied will be intreperted as, and that intreptation is final with little abitliy to recontextualize. 

This of course undermines any moral arguement the game attempts to present or have you consider. Over surveillance, the effect of technology on the governments ability to monitor it's citizens and so forth are good topics to explore. However demonstarting the conquences by forcing the player to pick up the idiot ball does no one any favours.  

The concept is good, if you can deal with being forced to make uncontextualized leaps of judgement you might enjoy the game. But the inability to use good inquirial practices like preserving and rexamining conflicting data in light of new evidence kills the game for me.

The game really takes you through the extremes of an orwellian state in disguise, which makes you more aware in general how realistic the topic might have become.

I really would advise anyone to play, albeit for the conclusion they draw from it themselves.

So I got this game for free on HB, and was eager to try it out. As I am a fan of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dystopia]dystopian[/url] novels and games. Fictions like [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four]1984[/url] or [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brave_New_World]Brave New World[/url] are what I'd love to read.

This game is based off George Orwell's 1984(hence the game's name [i]Orwell[/i]). A government launching a surveillance system in a bid to stop "terrorists" and their "attacks". You are one of the agents that helps submitting [i]correct[/i] information to government intel. Suspects will be arrested or able to escape from arrestments based on what information you provided. Much like [url=https://store.steampowered.com/agecheck/app/475550/]Beholder[/url], you can save innocents or those you want to help by not submitting certain data to the Orwell system.

After a few minutes into the game, I decide that this game is quite worth the pennies. It allows you to experience being a "Big Brother" - watching citizens behind, logging every moves they make, and determining their ultimate fate. Although the Big Brother perspective is already popular among dystopian games. I find this one quite interesting. Unlike beholder, you don't need to go around maintaining good terms with residents. Instead you sit right in front of a surveillance system, pretty much like the real world NSA agents would do in their everyday work.

To sum up, I would recommend this game to everyone. Still thinking your privacy is REALLY SAFE online? On the fence of thinking about being spyed on? Play this game.
